Ultralight bosonic dark matter (UBDM) can be represented as a nearly massless scalar or tensor field coupled weakly to standard model particles. Its ultra-slow velocity results in an almost constant field amplitude that slowly modulates over time at the frequency of its natural oscillation, potentially generating observable correlations between the fluctuating intensities of light from distinct detectors or fluctuations among repeated measurements of the same source. This signature, known as intensity interferometry, has been discussed for decades because it theoretically supports detection frequencies extending up to Hertz even for particle masses as high as $10^{-25}$ GeV/$c^2$. While existing literature has primarily concentrated on scenarios involving astrophysical DM emission, we address the more widespread scenario in which DM accumulates directly within the Earth or Solar System. Additionally, we clarify existing terminology and introduce several new intensity interferometry techniques tailored for direct detection. Specifically, this approach provides independent verification through measurement timing and offers complementary data when combined with differential methods used in direct detection experiments.

This study investigates the presence and behavior of unique solutions within the basis continuum and establishes that, for generic data vectors, the basis continuum minimization problem possesses a unique solution. This property aligns the basis continuum unique solvability with regression and smoothing spline minimization. We also examine related questions, including the connection between uniqueness and the structure of Lagrange multipliers, connection coefficients, and connection points, alongside the mark property of the partition of the continuum induced by these points. Additionally, we address polynomial interpolation within the mean square norm and demonstrate through examples from smoothing spline theory and the basis continuum that unique solvability is not a generic trait in those settings.

The P4 language has established itself as the leading choice for configuring switched infrastructure, supporting the rapid development of new protocols and switch features while fostering compatibility through unified abstract syntax. Although numerous P4 compilers exist, they largely focus on generating front-end functionality for parsing, tokenizing, and generating code, frequently using only standard libraries for the back-end because these components vary widely by target hardware and programming languages, necessitating significant development effort to implement correctly. We introduce an open-source P4 back-end tailored for data plane reconfigurable switches, specifically designed to produce code compliant with the V1.0 of the P16 architecture. This component utilizes existing standard libraries rather than developing them from scratch. By using established resources, this project aims to alleviate development burdens for other users of the P4 language.

In finite element simulations of incompressible fluid flow, the accuracy of the solution depends significantly on the discretization of the vector transport equation. In this study, a high-precision approximation is proposed for this equation when utilizing the lowest-order Raviart-Thomas elements on quadrilateral meshes. The suggested method achieves this by reformulating the transport term so that it can be computed using scalar functions that admit accurate numerical integration via standard two-dimensional cubic rules. When paired with standard element-wise mass matrices, this approach yields improved flow field results. The effectiveness of the proposed method is confirmed through experimental validation on diverse and complex mesh topologies.

The significant achievements driven by deep learning have introduced numerous ethical challenges, including algorithmic bias and threats to data privacy. To confront these problems, scholars employ techniques such as fairness evaluation metrics, federated learning architectures, and differential privacy. Initial research presented here introduces an ethical model integrating these three strategies simultaneously and uses experimentation across the Adult, Bank, and Dutch data sets to illuminate how a practical balance exists among accuracy, fairness, and privacy.

Through a novel training scheme designed to optimize all networks, demonstrated its application on ResNet-50 utilizing 128 GPUs. Three-dimensional chaotic scattering was previously believed to generate Wada basins exclusively in the absence of dissipation; however, the discovery presented herein demonstrates that weak dissipation can in fact generate and enlarge Wada basisms in both two and three dimensions. This analysis focuses on the classic model of low-dissipation three-dimensional scattering before examining its Wada boundary structures and the sensitivity of these boundaries by examining how they shift with varying dissipative parameters.

We examine an Effective field theory framework involving two light scalar bosons, $B$ and $S$. While $B$ drives light-dark dark energy through accidental stability, it decays into $S$ via a Yukawa interaction. $S$ functions as a decay product capable of generating both dark energy and observable phenomena. We investigate whether this model can reproduce Hubble-induced non-standard recombination signatures and derive corresponding limits from both microlensing observations and laboratory experiments. We determine that for mass ratios where the parameter $\epsilon = m_{S}/m_{B}$ is significantly less than one, the parameter space is largely permitted by astrophysical bounds, located between Baryon Abundance Enhancement (BAE) and Stability-Modified Gravity (SMG) constraints. This viable region allows BAE to manifest as a signal in microlensing and for SMG to be detected in recombination while remaining within regulatory limits.

Recognizing human activities in unposed video is a challenging task with broad significance across media monitoring, medical and military applications, as well as security. While current state-of-the-art image-based recognition methods focus heavily on global context and semantic cues essential for activity identification, these visual cues often lack consistency across single frames due to variations in timing, observation angles, and environmental factors. Although incorporating multiple frames can bolster semantic and contextual diversity, traditional video methods struggle to balance these diverse inputs effectively. Addressing this input heterogeneity is a critical step toward robust action recognition. Consequently, this study introduces a Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN) designed to process varied video inputs while explicitly modeling long-term temporal dependencies for action classification. Crucially, HAN features a hierarchical attention mechanism that simultaneously highlights important regions within individual frames and filters significant intervals throughout the entire video sequence. Experimental evaluations on the UCF101 and UBACAction datasets indicate that the HAN model exceeds existing state-of-the-art performance in action recognition.

The dynamics of the non-extremal Reissner-Nordstr$\ddot{o}$m anti-de Sitter black hole dynamics, specifically the temporal variations in mass, charge, and radius, are investigated within this work. By employing a external, time-dependent scalar field, we derive consistent evolution equations for the black hole's mass and charge. Our analysis confirms that all cons quantities remain within bounds consistent with the first and second laws of thermodynamics. Additionally, we verify that the weakest world-protection conjecture holds true in this context.

Consequently, the entire inquiry regarding life throughout the universe and its origins can be approached from an innovative standpoint.

While Shannon entropy and associated metrics, such as mutual information, serve to quantify the significance of alterations within biological systems, their estimation remains challenging when dealing with discrete configurations of vast state spaces. Consequently, this paper proposes leveraging Nested Sampling to calculate these metric estimators in extensive systems. Since this technique inherently provides estimates for numerous other statistics relevant to statistical physics, the authors introduce a new algorithm specifically designed to estimate mutual information. Additionally, synthetic experiments utilizing models for RNA secondary structures and protein folds confirm that the predicted probability distributions closely approximate true distributions, with the model demonstrating enhanced performance compared to traditional Monte Carlo methods.

Cyclades is an experimental testbed designed to investigate innovative classifications for detecting network intrusions on embedded devices with constrained resources. While current mainstream solutions focus on converting network packets into TCP or JSON sequences for analysis, these methods demand excessive memory and processing power, rendering them unsuitable for legacy hardware such as firewalls based on the ProSafe 500N. To address this limitation, our proposal encoded packet sequences using a sequence-to-sequence neural model into fixed memory sizes. These stored representations were then fed into a Naive Bayes classifier for classifying embedded attack types. The Cyclades framework, operated on a ProSafe 500N device, demonstrated full detection of the 2013 Extended Dataset attacks. Initial performance analysis indicated that our solution memory- and energy-outperforms the EBPM method while delivering comparable results. The Cyclades framework can be accessed via https://github.com/lorenzo-ferretti/Cyclades.

Optimizing power grid operations and settings is vital for minimizing operational expenses and seamlessly integrating renewable energy sources. This study introduces a quantum algorithm that offers an exact solution to network optimization challenges. By leveraging features like superposition and entanglement within the quantum framework, this approach shows significant potential for delivering performance gains over existing classical methods.

The rapid expansion in the volume of experimental and observational data has fueled substantial progress in data science and statistical analysis across science and engineering. A primary ambition in this field is to uncover fundamental laws of nature directly from data, given that the rigorous derivation of these laws and their corresponding mathematical models from first principles remains extremely difficult, if not impossible, within many scenarios. We propose that discovering these laws can be decomposed into two distinct phases: (i) identifying discrepancies between predicted and actual data, and (ii) uncovering the underlying models designed to eliminate these inconsistencies. Within this framework, we introduce a novel data-driven methodology for deriving physical laws, consisting of two core elements. Firstly, we utilize the discrepancy identification step, implemented via a universal signature known as a universal functional based on the statistical distance known as the Wasserstein metric. Secondly, we employ generalization techniques from contemporary machine learning to detect and eliminate discrepancies, thereby deriving the specific mathematical models. Regarding the discrepancy identification phase, we demonstrate that the universal functional based on the Wasserstein metric effectively captures discrepancies regardless of the data type (discrete, vectorial, or tensorial), the nature of the variables (deterministic or stochastic), or the underlying physical laws. Furthermore, we establish theoretical proofs for the second framework element by establishing upper limits on the prediction errors when using deep neural networks, high-dimensional methods, and functional networks. This study details a search conducted by the ATLAS detector at the LHC for hypothetical heavy, electrically charged particles with long lifetimes, utilizing a data set with an integrated luminosity of $139\ \text{fb}^{-1}$ collected from proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13\ \text{teV}$. Because such particles move slower than the speed of light and generate significant particle showers, they are identified primarily through anomalously high specific energy loss ($\d\epsilon/\d\x$). The analysis employs two complementary identification techniques to detect these objects: a heuristic strategy and a specialized template fitting method based on a $\d\epsilon/\d\x$ distribution. Both approaches show consistency with the standard model, allowing for constraints on the production rates of charged, stable particles with lifetimes exceeding one centimeter to be established at a $95\%$ confidence level. The study further reports sensitivity to specific new physics models, including those featuring confined dark sectors or hadrons formed from dark sectors, or massive axin-like particles coupled weakly to standard model forces through one-photon interactions.

Meta-analyses often include trials with multiple associated studies, creating within-trial correlations that necessitate the use of robust methods for accurate inference. Particle-resolved simulation methods, including discrete element method, are employed to analyze multi-particle systems exhibiting diverse time scales, such as those involving particles with varying sizes or different friction characteristics. Ensuring program correctness is crucial for systems. Historically for general-purpose computing and High-Performance Computing (HPC), software was written for Volatile Memory where algorithm crash consistency was key, as data could be easily restored upon system failures. In this work, we present an algorithm transformation method designed to automatically generate NVM-compatible versions for HPC applications while maintaining high performance and ensuring consistency across different execution environments. By analyzing 22 benchmarks from the NAS HPC suite, we demonstrate that our solution NVM-adapts 96% to 100% of the tested algorithms, resulting in comparable crash consistency and performance rates across NVM and Volitional Memory architectures.

Understanding the multiphase flow topology is crucial for interpreting flow data and creating accurate multiphase turbulence models. This study introduces a novel approach that represents the three-dimensional multiphase flow topology using skeletons. Unlike traditional methods that rely on level-sets to define interfaces, this technique constructs interfaces by fitting analytical surface functions, resulting in smoother, lower-computation interfaces suitable for capturing complex three-phase structures. By converting the resulting interface normals into a 5-nearest-neighbor connectivity graph, this method explicitly reconstructs the topological characteristics. Its validity has been demonstrated through two cases: a straightforward scenario involving three slabs flowing side-by-side and a more complex case of three droplets moving together.

Recent research has revealed that the Spherical Buckle (SB) nanovirus self-rolls under gravity across horizontal surfaces, executing complex trajectories that mirror those of larger rolling objects. While such sustained viral movement could facilitate the transport of mechanical energy and perform internal work conducive to their self-assembly, the underlying mechanical mechanisms remained uncertain. This study reveals that multilegged viruses like the SB behave akin to two-legged pod robots, where both symmetry and leg count are critical for enabling self-sustaining rolling. Specifically, symmetry ensures stable rotation, whereas leg count determines trajectory complexity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that adjusting the phase of activation among legs allows us to enhance traversal efficiency and energy usage, thereby improving the effective mechanical work performed. This research provides earlier observations and fresh insights into how symmetry and leg count influence the mechanics of self-sustained rolling in the SB nanovirus.

We present AccoPose, which enhances 3D object pose estimation by leveraging additional input: a "turntable" image series of an object around a specific axis. COPASI is a widely utilized, multi-platform scientific tool for analyzing dynamics in bio-medical systems. Although capable of handling extensive models, its command-line and graphical desktop interfaces can be challenging for tasks focused on exploration, visualization, teaching, demonstrating results, or developing new ideas, particularly when compared to the limitations of its current remote access options which rely on expensive dedicated server access. To address this, we introduce ShinyCOPASI, a user-friendly, browser-based interface designed to run COPASI models locally on the client's machine via HTTP/HTTPS. Running within anyone's web browser, ShinyCOPASI enables rapid and efficient investigation of dynamic systems through interactive control over simulation settings such as initial concentrations, kinetic rates, visualization formats, supported graph types, or even linked network data. Its intuitive design effectively supports exploration, instructional purposes, and the demonstration of computational findings, with network visualization capabilities powered by NetworkViz and its integration with network data structures facilitated through Sarbi.

Neural networks are capable of modeling diverse complex physical systems. Nevertheless, when employing them for this purpose, there exists an inherent risk that point predictions may result in erroneous results caused by issues such as imperfect training data, limited network capacity, poor initialization, insufficient iterations, points outside of the training distribution, or inadequate optimization. This uncertainty may lead to flawed decision-making scenarios and has thus become a critical area within the machine learning community. While Bayesian methods have historically been the primary framework for global uncertainty quantification (UQ) in conventional finite element analysis (FEA), they often face computational challenges related to scalability. A potential alternative for this task is point-based uncertainty quantification; however, these approaches have received minimal attention within the physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) framework. This study introduces various novel methods for uncertainty quantification using scientific machine learning. We provide an extensive validation across diverse problems with extensive data. The proposed uncertainty quantification methods are evaluated against commonly used metrics for both deterministic and stochastic outputs.

In the context of compact quantum groups, we examine analogues of the radial subalgebras found in free group factors, specifically the algebras of class functions. Regarding free orthogonal quantum groups, we demonstrate that the algebra of class functions constitutes a maximal subalgebra which is both abelian and finite-type. Conversely, when focusing on the quantum $SU(2)$ group, the algebra of class functions fails to be a factor. Additionally, we construct a family of quantum groups featuring class function subalgebras that define proper von Neumann algebras.

Interest in solving extensive Markov chain systems of linear equations has risen notably due to their capacity to identify stationary distributions, a trend that policy iteration extends similarly for solving large-scale Markov models for reaching steady-state quality assessments. Although shown previously to mirror the general policy iteration approach in being extremely efficient for certain dense Markov problems, this specific algorithm requires reduction in computational costs for scalability. Our work focuses on minimizing computational costs for large-scale Markov decision problems. We suggest an accelerated iterative technique that integrates several features from previous efficient approaches for both matrix equation resolution in Markov chains and policy iterations. By incorporating the GMRES approach into this iteration, the resulting algorithm is shown to be more space-efficient than other iterations. Our findings are supported by a theoretical basis for the convergence of this approach, and the efficiency of the method is demonstrated in various cases of large-scale Markov problems.

Computer models are frequently substituted for complex physical systems to analyze responses to varying parameter sets. This approach is particularly effective when the model's response characteristics are smooth, the input dimensionality is relatively low, and available sample sizes are modest. Both artificial datasets and real-world examples demonstrate that the MCE-based technique yields reliable inferences regarding the input parameters.

This study investigates scenarios in robust learning where learning algorithms permit only local queries—requests restricted to a small, constant-radius neighborhood within the input space. We also expand the previous results by showing how learning algorithms can remain effective within the real number field, rather than relying on structures like robust finite fields, thereby opening new avenues for understanding local query applications in Euclidean geometry.

Crewed lunar and Martian exploration necessitates both bringing back samples and bringing in people. While some tasks require human astronauts, others could instead be handled by robotic agents, which have lower risks and higher efficiency. A key task involves creating 3D-printed habitats using local regolith, which demands materials with high strength and good workability. This study aimed to optimize the sintering temperature to achieve such material properties by compacting and sintering regolith simulant under varying temperatures. Both lunar and Martian simulant were compacted at pressures ranging from 0.05 to 0.3 MPa and then heated at temperatures between 623 K and 1073 K. Our results indicate that the optimal combination for mimicking Mars is a pressure of 0.05 MPa and a temperature of 873 K, which produces a granular microstructure with quartz, feldspar, and vitreous phases, yielding an unconfined compressive strength (UCS) of 1.03±0.10 MPa. The behavior of a liquid film flowing along a fiber relies fundamentally on conditions at the liquid-solid interface, which is commonly characterized by slip. In this study, we perform analyses including numerical simulations and analytical investigations into how slip accelerates the Rayleigh-Plateau instability of the cylindrical film. It is observed that, regardless of the specific flow equations employed, increasing slip intensity consistently amplifies disturbances, leading to stronger perturbations, shorter wavelength ripples, and greater growth rates. Furthermore, we provide analytical evidence showing that slip promotes instabilities by reducing boundary energy dissipation, thereby enhancing the transfer of kinetic energy to disturbance amplitudes. Our findings further indicate that while alternative flow models yield different base profiles, their reliance on slip to drive instability enhances both the stability of the cylindrical configuration and the feasibility of our conclusions.

By comparing observations of the $\lambda$2.16\(\mu\)m Brackett-\(\gamma\) (Br\(\gamma\)) line with broad-band photometry in 14 nearby galaxies, we assessed whether broadband spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting yields reliable star formation rates (SFR). We find that while Br\(\gamma\)-derived SFR correlations with broadband fluxes are generally consistent, they suffer from significant uncertainties, particularly in galaxies with B$< -15$. In these systems, we observe a scatter of a factor of three, accompanied by a slope that is both shallower and offset from unity. These uncertainties are largely attributable to the blue/UV extinction properties and age of stellar populations, which cause variations in broadband flux ratios. Conversely, because Br\(\gamma\)-based SFR estimates rely solely on near-infrared fluxes, they remain largely independent of UV extinction or age. Consequently, when broad-band data are lacking, or when galaxies are young, infrared observations like Br\(\gamma\)-derived fluxes offer a more dependable means of calculating SFR. Specifically, for understanding the early phases of galaxy evolution, such as star and black hole formation, we argue that the Br\(\gamma\)-derived method serves as the appropriate gold-standard benchmark.

The critical role of dermatologists in diagnosing skin lesions, particularly skin cancer, is underscored by the fact that these lesions represent the most prevalent form of cancer among humans, detectable and treatable if identified at an early stage via the skin. Detecting lesions often requires specialized training, which has led to this publication introducing the "Skincare" project, an interactive Deep Learning (DL) tool designed to assist in the differential diagnosis of skin cancer cases. By leveraging state-of-the-art DL architectures and diagnostic reasoning, the Skincare project delivers interpretable explanations for its outputs to aid medical professionals effectively. Furthermore, this technical report examines the evolution of the system and delineates its prospective applications within the field.

We develop a probabilistic autoencoder (PAE) to analyze the evolution of Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) by processing multi-band spectroscopic time series. These SNe Ia serve as critical standardizable candles for measuring cosmological distances across vast scales; their observed brightness depends on redshift. Understanding their pre-explosion evolution may help refine distance estimates. Our PAE model extracts latent features characterizing this evolution from complex spectral data while accounting for both continuous variables (e.g., velocity, abundance) and discrete variables (e.g., explosion delays, rise times) associated with a sample of 1,049 PAEMs observed by the Astrophoto Spectroscopic Survey of Type Ia Supernovae (ASTROSNET). We validate findings through predictive modeling of cosmological distance modes and evaluate them against a simpler linear encoder-decoder architecture. Results indicate that the PAEM effectively isolates independent latent variables, accurately forecasting continuous functions (such as expansion velocities) at specific wavelengths and explosion rise times, and effectively predicts explosion dates when supplied with both spectral data and known occurrence dates to distinguish potential subtypes and measure cosmological distances.

Using ALMA Band 3 observations, we measured the outflow's velocity structure through high signal-to-noise ratio data. After applying a model-based subtraction of the gravitational lens, the true outflow was uncovered, revealing that it is highly resolved, with an effective outflow radius of R_eff = 2.4 ± 0.1 kpc. Laboratory experiments were conducted to examine the entrainment of the ambient fluid by growing turbulent plumes in particle-laden fluids. In these experiments, fresh plumes were introduced into a quiescent water column containing rising salt particles, while the corresponding salt-plumes formed within a fluid of zero viscosity were also investigated to establish context. Utilizing two complementary imaging techniques, two-dimensional plumes were captured and analyzed. Broad-side views visualized both the coherent plume core and particle distribution, whereas top-down perspectives mapped particle concentrations. Leveraging data from both views, researchers quantified how local entrainment rates vary along the plume. The findings indicate entrainment scales follow a power law with respect to the local Reynolds number but remain largely unaffected by the Bond number. Furthermore, when normalized by fresh fluid concentration, both the mean entrainment rate and its fluctuation intensity display consistent behavior across varying Reynolds numbers. These experimental results were compared with leading theoretical models proposed for multi-component plumes.

Observations indicate that as stars age, the rate of differential rotation among solar-type stars reaches a peak and declines due to the transition from cyclonic to turbidlent flows induced by super-adiabatic gradients. Consequently, we investigate how the presence of anti-solar differential rotation (ADR), where equatorial regions rotate more slowly than polar regions, influences the open-flux fraction and magnetic activity cycles. Utilizing 3D global convection simulations for systems exhibiting both solar-differential rotation (SDR) and ADR, we observed significant variations in open flux levels across the magnetic spectrum (ranging from $10^7$ to $10^9$ Gauss). To address this, we developed an empirical model based on open flux vs. angular velocity data, which aligns well with existing observational datasets. We then applied this model to measure the cycles in four HD stars—rotating at ages of 60, 90, 150, and 200 million years—which mark the onset of ADR. For these systems, our findings suggest that the anti-solar differential rotation has only a negligible effect on the lifespan of magnetic cycles.

Multimodal deep Boltzmann machines (DBMs) have become a significant advancement in cross-modality information sharing within computer vision, largely due to their unidirectional architecture, which facilitates efficient parallel training. Nevertheless, due to their reliance on back-propagation for training, they struggle with deeper networks, which hampers the full utilization of deep hierarchical features. Consequently, enhancing the training of these deeper networks through more effective, mode-centric strategies has emerged as a critical, unresolved challenge at the core of multimodal deep learning. Addressed through a novel Generalized K-Fan architecture tailored specifically for multimodal environments, the proposed method enhances deep modeling and improves intermodality feature integration by employing shared representations and implementing effective layer-wise unsupervised pre-training. Empirical validation across diverse datasets confirms that the generalized K-fan framework consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches.

Model checking has emerged as a key technique for verifying multi-threaded programs by exploring their state spaces to detect bugs, though approaches that consider program history to reduce redundant state exploration often struggle with complex control flows and lack clear guidelines for scaling to large applications. To address these issues, we introduce McMini, a model checker grounded in DPOR (Dynamic Partial Order Reduction) designed for C programs using mutexes for synchronization. McMini achieves significant reductions in both memory usage and runtime by leveraging compact, precise per-thread dependencies that drive targeted predicate abstraction. Evaluations across various real-world benchmarks demonstrate that, relative to prior model checking and static analysis tools, McMini delivers comprehensive semantic coverage while offering substantial improvements in performance and efficiency.

Nonreciprocal optical systems are widely used to manipulate the signal transmission of light based on its travel direction, but in this study, we investigate a new type of nonreciprocity that manifests specifically within photon pair correlations rather than linear propagation. This phenomenon represents a reversible behavior in the second-order coherence functions of entangled photon pairs generated via spontaneous four-wave mixing on a silicon microdisk, as confirmed by both experimental and theoretical evidence. Crucially, inverting the direction of the pumping beam causes significant suppression of these coherence functions while remaining independent of any magnetic fields or materials that typically drive nonreciprocal effects.

Superconducting quantum circuits are recognized as a promising platform for building quantum computers. Achieving crucial components like nearly "one-shot readout," higher fidelity operations, and correcting quantum errors requires coherence times that are orders of magnitude longer than currently available. We contend that near-field terahertz imaging can assist in attaining these necessary improvements across superconducting quantum processing. Our work demonstrates the capability of Terahertz Scanning Microwave Microscopy (TSAM) to probe frequencies up to 1.5 THz within superconductive quantum loop systems. We demonstrated the capability to resolve spatial features as small as ~200 nm and correlated these measurements with numerical simulations. The spatial precision achieved allows for characterizing local losses arising from materials other than bulk superconductiveness, specifically within the immediate vicinity of quantum circuits. By identifying such sources of dissipation, engineers can work toward further loss reduction and enhance circuit performance.

Electrostatic gating effectively controls semiconductors and CTCs within superconductors, yet generating spin currents remains elusive, even in systems with inherent ferromagnetism. This study reveals that gating low-bilby-temperature superconductors in close proximity to magnets enables direct spin flux modulation. Under ideal conditions, carriers crossing the superconducting interface absorb and re-emit magnons—the collective spin excitations—from neighbors. Because superconducting carriers possess a significantly longer lifetime than magnetic spin waves, electrons can absorb individual spin photons one-by-one from ambient sources. Superconducting proximity effects further amplify the lifetime, allowing electrons to function as efficient rectifiers of magnonic flow. Neighboring superconducting regions offer tunable spin injection strength via electrostatic fields. Empirical data from van der Waals heterostructures (specifically CrI2 and NbSe2) validates this mechanism, where applying a gate voltage to NbSe2 successfully switched off the spin flux generated by CrI2 with nearly complete efficiency. These findings establish three distinct interfaces to produce, switch on, and modulate magnonic signals for future spintronics applications.

Federated learning for new class deployment and zero‑shotted cross-domain classification are both challenged by a lack of client labels and training data outside the domain. These issues are especially pronounced when clients gather diverse, high-quality datasets for training foundational AI models—a task that frequently fails due to real-world constraints. To address this, we introduce a unified federated learning framework combining multiple techniques to handle emerging categories and apply it to a zero‑shotted music genre classification study. Key elements include: (1) a heterogeneous data collection and aggregation system that operates without needing local dataset updates; (2) a class embedding technique that utilizes unlabeled data; and (3) a class‑embedding guided model that enables updates via dataset exchanges while maintaining robust generalization despite limited local samples. Demonstrating the approach on a zero‑shotted audio dataset, we show that our method surpasses current state‑of‑the‑art performance by 4.4 percentage points; furthermore, we observe that the training process remains reliable even with heterogeneous data collection, incurring only an insignificant decrease in accuracy accompanied by accelerated convergence rates.

This Letter introduces a theoretical framework designed for comprehensive optical analysis of high-dimensional Greenberger-Horne-Zeinberger (GHZ) resources. The study initially validates this methodology through complete measurements of distinct three-photon GHZ states within a tripartite quantum basis. The approach is subsequently generalized, with a full photonic hyper-entanglement and quantum Fourier transform integration. The utility of this proposal extends towards enhanced multi-photon capabilities for both quantum computing and quantum communications in higher-order dimensions of entanglement.

This paper investigates a reflection-assisted multiple-user single-output system designed to compensate for large-scale blockages by integrating intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS). The proposed framework features a decentralized architecture where IRS channel parameters are estimated through a cascaded method, while user channel estimates are derived via maximum likelihood (ML) estimation. To address the non-convex nature of the associated optimization challenge, a distributed algorithm based on alternating optimization is introduced. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme enhances sum rates compared to baseline methods and exhibits faster convergence than competing estimation algorithms.

We analyze how local U.S. online newspaper subscriptions and audience figures responded during the early COVID-19 pandemic. Case counts and death tolls showed a clear seasonal increase, peaking in August 2020 before declining slightly; this increase coincided with rising reading rates among residents aged 50 and older and, to a lesser degree, those younger than 50. These findings indicate that COVID-1️₎ news consumption was tightly linked to the epidemic's severity and progression. Notably, while subscription numbers remained stable, online readership grew over the course of the pandemic. We offer these results as motivation for policymakers to continue monitoring COVID-1️₣ coverage levels and its societal effects.

Counting is a vital milestone in both acquiring language and marking developmental progress. Although its significance within cognitive evolution is clear, understanding *how* it emerges remains unresolved. This study proposes an agent-based framework to investigate counting acquisition, leveraging deep learning techniques that integrate human cognitive insights. We introduce Memory-Augmented Neural Networks (MANNs) with integrated bias layers to model counting as a Labeled Markov Decision Process (LMDP), effectively capturing both internal state changes and external system state transitions. Our analysis, supported by controlling experiments, demonstrates that biasing these layers yields more accurate count predictions and higher internal representation quality compared to unsupervised models. Additionally, we explore how specific bias configurations align with distinct cognitive capabilities, such as aphantasia, to ensure that the emerging skills are truly cognitive in nature.

Bloom filters efficiently manage fast, approximate membership checks for sets of data values. Over time, two other approaches have emerged with better theoretical time complexities: standard Cuckoo filters, which guarantee constant-average insertion and retrieval times, and Xor filters, which offer linear-scaling performance relative to both inserted values and stored counts. Despite these theoretical advantages in practice, both filter types have been considered slower and larger than their Bloom filter counterparts for real-world datasets. Our research presents enhanced Xor filter data structures with improved practical performance, providing both faster operation and smaller footprints. Our work is supported by rigorous theoretical analysis as well as experimental data gathered across diverse datasets.

Federated learning (FL) stands out as a promising and privacy-secure machine learning framework ensuring data retention within client locations. Despite these advantages, widespread FL adoption remains hindered by two main hurdles: malicious clients capable of corrupting global models through deceptive updates and the leakage of data via standard gradient sharing. Various solutions have emerged to mitigate these specific risks, yet no prior method successfully addresses them both simultaneously. In response, this paper introduces FLVoogd, a novel system that combines a variation of the Voigd filter for data cleaning with advanced encoding/decoding techniques designed for secure communication. Beyond their individual utility, both mechanisms are adapted to enable robust and privacy-preserving federated learning. Experimental results demonstrate that FLVoogd surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in both resilience and privacy protection. Additionally, the framework is extensible to support data heterogeneity and dynamic network environments.

We have created a new algorithm called "Ours," designed to transfer neural network models directly from simulated to real-world driving environments. Unlike many existing approaches that need to fine-tune on real data using small real data sets, our method eliminates the need for such datasets during the fine-tuning process entirely. Instead, Ours employs a loss function that minimizes the discrepancy between a gradient of a simulated neural network and a gradient of a simulated one, applied to a data augmentation strategy that pairs simulated network outputs (e.g., predicted paths) with corresponding real-world images to create a "real data proxy." By training exclusively on synthetic data and refining the network using this real data proxy, our method is able to learn robust, real-world-applicable features without exposure to real datasets during the refinement stage. Experiments indicate that Ours achieves a lower generalization error than the baseline method and competes effectively with cutting-edge unsupervised and self-supervised techniques. Additionally, our model is capable of producing reliable lane detection, vehicle position tracking, and estimated heading for unseen autonomous driving data.

Recent leaps in deep learning catalysis notable enhancements to deepfake creation, culminating in counterfeits that exhibit heightened realism. It further examines methods aimed at bolstering the reliability of detection algorithms across diverse media formats (such as authenticating unsanctioned images and footage), ultimately recommending priorities for forthcoming investigations into deceptive media technologies.

The paper proposes a framework for the retrospective assessment of generalized polynomial chaos (GPCC) expansions used to solve differential equations featuring random parameters. The approach combines GPCC solution representations, where random variables are replaced by stochastic expansion coefficients, with the coefficient optimization method, typically least squares. When these elements are integrated, the problem addresses the intersection between two key concepts, namely how the coefficients are optimized and the random variables are represented. The analysis reveals that if a GPCC solution exists, it must be both necessary and sufficient. Furthermore, under specific conditions, it can be proven that the problem remains equivalent to one with randomly shifted polynomial degrees, utilizing a technique known as random shift equivalence. By establishing this equivalence and performing the transformation, the original validation issue is converted into a deterministic one. To handle the resulting determinism, the study adapts existing methods for validating deterministic problems, extending their use to handle the newly created random shift context so that the validation can be completed. Numerical examples are provided to demonstrate both the theoretical findings and the effectiveness of the proposed methodology in validating problems such as the random heat equation.

The previously successful partiality (PA) algorithm is recognized as a leading strategy for anomaly detection and isolation in single sensory systems. Nevertheless, when applied to platforms involving sequential multi-sensor observations with a multi-dimensional state, its performance is constrained by heavy computational requirements and strict reliance on predetermined system parameters. To address these limitations, we present the adaptive partiality (AP) method, which implements the core principles of PA within a directionally adaptive filter framework capable of tracking trends across multiple observation axes. The AP algorithm is demonstrated to be effective for both anomaly detection and threshold evaluation through application to 1D and 3D test scenarios.

This study investigates the stellar ages, metallicity, and specific elemental abundances in 13 nearby dwarf galaxies utilizing data from the APOGEE survey. We achieve this through individual spectroscopic analysis of 114,030 nearby stars, resulting in new chemical abundance estimates for 10 of these dwarfs and confirming previously published values for the other two: WS200 and S0220. By examining basic chemical abundance patterns and mass-dependent trends, we find little variation among these dwarfs. For instance, iron-group and $\alpha$-element abundances follow a single-slope power law relative to metallicity, with modest variations in low-metallicity regimes. However, magnesium-to-iron ratios exhibit a clear dependence on galaxy mass. Additionally, our abundance patterns suggest these dwarf galaxies possessed super-solar oxygen production, indicative of significant nucleosynthesis involving massive stars. Finally, we observe significant discrepancies between predicted chemical trends and actual measurements, implying that most dwarf galaxies experienced early, rapid shifts in their star formation modes.

Building accurate automatic extraction models for visual-heavy documents, such as invoices, is significantly hampered by the expensive collection of thousands of well- annotated training samples required for robust performance. Deciding how to optimally allocate resources within a framework of constraints presents significant practical challenges across numerous fields. A core example is introducing limits on the anticipated or severe impact of a decision on various societal groups. A primary method for tackling this issue is formating it as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP). A CMDP involves determining a stationary policy for a standard Markov Decision Process (MDD) in order to maximize its total discounted reward, while ensuring predicted expected costs remain below a specific threshold. Although optimal solutions for CMDPs exist, existing literature relies on techniques that are difficult to implement: they typically require the ability to compute the probability distribution of the total expected cost for every potential policy and then execute a constrained optimization procedure to select a valid one. In this paper, we present a novel method for solving CMDPs that circumvents the need for pre-computing cost distributions. Instead, we frame CMDPs as a zero-sum two-player zero-sum game involving a decision-maker aiming to maximize a modified version of the reward, playing against a constraint-enemy whose goal is to maximize their own costs. We develop a novel, externally event-triggered Primal-Dual Algorithm to resolve these games, and numerical evaluations on both synthetic examples and a practical logistics application demonstrate that this approach outperforms traditional methods by being not only faster but also easier to deploy.

The Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) forms a dense disk within our Galaxy. To investigate the density anatomy of such disks, researchers have turned to the approach proposed by Klyachko et al. Quantum information circuits primarily function by logically processing stable qubits using linear optical components and quantum measurement. However, because of the linearity of light, implementing non-linear qubit operations has remained a persistent obstacle. In this paper, we employ a pair of quantum scissors to demonstrate the generation of polarization entanglement. Moreover, we utilize quantum error correction techniques to ensure that the resulting entangled state maintains high purity. Experimentally, our method produces an entangled polarization purity of 0.96 and achieves successful rates exceeding 30%. Importantly, our approach mandates that only two-photon detection is necessary rather than requiring the detection of every photon. This provides an economical and efficient pathway to create photonic entanglement, facilitating the development of quantum computing using light.

Classifying IoT devices into specific categories is critical for identifying potential security risks. While recent studies have shown that analyzing packet features is more effective than maintaining security software databases for device classification, extracting these features usually requires specialized hardware, which is often unavailable. To address this limitation, we present a method to identify the most cost-efficient subset of features that maximizes classification accuracy without needing dedicated hardware. The approach begins by quantifying the cost of acquiring each feature, taking into account the variable capture rates and individual payload sizes. Using this definition, we apply the Random Forest classifier to rank features based on their mutual information score, then systematically evaluate every possible feature combination to determine the optimal subset. Experimental results indicate that this solution identifies a feature subset capable of achieving comparable or superior results to the full feature set. Moreover, the findings demonstrate that even the top-ranked single feature can significantly outperform previous approaches found in the literature.

Standard imaging requires light to interact with an object and be captured by a sensor. However, as quantum optics progresses, researchers explore ways to manipulate light at the quantum level, potentially replacing traditional components like beamsplitters and mirrors. This setup compares scenarios with and without the object by examining the final detector outcomes, effectively using undetected photons for interaction-free imaging.

In ISIC 2019, a collection of 12,626 images was presented to participants for classifying skin lesions as either malignant or benign. While deep learning has emerged as a prominent solution for this challenge, submissions often struggled to achieve top results because the dataset contains outlier samples that confuse standard classifiers. To address this confusion, the current study introduces a method designed to detect anomalies and filter out these data outliers prior to prediction, beginning by estimating image entropy to gauge the degree of fine detail. Since high entropy indicates rich information while low entropy suggests a lack of specificity, it proves that the majority class images generally exhibit lower entropy compared to the minority class. Using a K-means-based approach, the authors then classify each image's entropy level to categorize it as either an anomaly or a normal instance. Subsequently, the merged dataset is partitioned into eight balanced stratified subsets to ensure representative sampling. Finally, a binary classifier is trained exclusively on eight non-anomatory subset images to predict whether each skin lesion is cancerous or safe, achieving an accuracy of approximately ninety-four percent.

We conduct a systematic investigation into the long-term spatial dynamics and state-specific statistical distributions of one-dimensional quantum walks defined by a three-state coin. Across various initial conditions, we demonstrate that the statistical profiles conform to a $\text{Beta}(1/2, d)$ distribution in one and two dimensions, as well as a $\text{Beta}(1/4, d)$ distribution in three dimensions, where the spatial dimension is denoted as $d$. These findings indicate distinct universal scaling behaviors, position-dependent diffusion, and power-law characteristics in both real and reciprocal spaces. Notably, the initial state has negligible impact on these asymptotic statistics, except when starting exclusively in the coin's eigenbasis states.

This paper investigates the advantages gained by applying self-supervised learning to Vision Transformers (ViT) when compared to Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) on visual tasks. To this end, it examines linear probes of CNN In21e and ViT models trained with different self-supervised strategies, including SimCLR, MoCo, BERT, and BEART. The results indicate that while all methods benefit from training, the ENMA augmentation approach combined with BEERT achieves the most substantial improvements across CNNS and ViTs alike. Detailed comparisons reveal that ViT generates higher-quality representations than CNN In21e specifically within the representation layers following SimCLR and MoCo training. While these models show strong performance in downstream tasks, the study demonstrates in detail that ViT self-supervised representations surpass CNN In21e across every network layer for both SimCLR and MoCo. Furthermore, a correlation exists between the fidelity of these representations and the advantages seen in upstream preprocessing or downstream applications.

We investigate a dissipative unified dark fluid incorporating both attractive and repulsive forces at the four-dimensional homogeneous cosmological level. In advance, we discuss the dissipative mechanisms driving this fluid's dynamical evolution. We identify four specific fixed-point solutions, analyzing their stability through an eigenvalue approach in the vicinity of these points. Beyond these solutions, we examine continuous trajectories that consistently pass through all four points. Specifically, we focus on a continuous, dissipative repulsive force characterized by anisotropic behavior under full non-linear analysis for the first time. We demonstrate that this force fulfills Allam et al.'s (2003) proposed criteria for exotic matter and, for the first time, provide evidence supporting the existence of dissipative unified dark fluid within anisometric universes.

Recent advancements in text-conditioned image generation diffusion models have attracted significant interest due to their impressive ability to produce realistic images from randomly typed prompts or random vector samples in text-space. Although such models offer powerful implicit editing capabilities, achieving consistent results within a short period of generation remains difficult. Consequently, there is a growing demand for more robust coherent editing techniques. In this paper, we investigate the generation process of these models and uncover the potential inherent in diffusion latent space for creating highly consistent random and coherent output. Our research demonstrates that diffusion latent space naturally supports stable artistic style transfer, allowing for consistent image generation across different style domains, such as turning photographs into stylized sketches. Additionally, we present ArtGuided, an articulated stable artistic editing framework, which enables precise manipulation of semantic content within images while preserving artistic style. Ultimately, our paper promises to open new avenues for exploring semantic-level, coherent artistic creation using style-guided editing techniques.

Recent breakthroughs in Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) have proven their efficacy across numerous machine learning domains, attracting significant interest. This study explores the application of BNNs in reversible steganography aimed at seamlessly embedding messages into natural images while preserving perfect recoverability of the carrier and the original content after message extraction. To achieve this, we introduce a novel BNN-based reversible steganography framework that maps input images to a posterior distribution of images containing encoded data. By sample-based extraction from this distribution, our method successfully embeds information with a high load capacity while maintaining quality, as demonstrated by experimental results on the Lloyd Markov textures and open-source images. Furthermore, we developed a post-processing technique that analyzes the pre-embedded image to further refine the output, achieving an even lower Mean Squared Error (MSE).

To investigate the capabilities and constraints of current dynamic recognition systems utilizing human minimal videos—also known as dynamic atomic videos (DATs)—we evaluated a collection of state-of-the-art CNN and RNN architectures against diverse test suites. Our findings confirm that these systems can master identifying DATs with a broad range of labels, a result achieved even after training solely on a single data set featuring only one hundred DATs identifying just twenty action classes. However, when presented with "impossible" DATs (a specific set of inputs deemed unintelligible to leading models), both existing architectures demonstrate an inability to process them effectively. To examine model limitations more deeply, we developed challenging challenges involving similar videos (those sharing label attributes) and confusing visual pairs (visual antonyms). On both fronts, current algorithms show poor performance. Ultimately, these empirical observations suggest that while existing models struggle with data efficiency and generalization concerning impossible inputs, there is urgent need for further research into improving robust dynamic action recognition.

When ordinary matter interacts with hidden sectors featuring Abelian gauge symmetry, kinetic mixing allows dark matter to be observed within our visible realm, with magnetic monopoles serving as a prime example of such a hidden charge carrier. Investigating the stability of the night sky under these conditions, we find stability if the kinetic mixing parameter is very weak (specifically $\epsilon^2 \sim 10^{-13}$), enabling the monopole to store energy monochromatically. Conversely, if the mixing is stronger ($\epsilon^2 \gtrsim 10^{-3}$), random mixing causes monopoles to accelerate, resulting in excessive emission. We propose that existing cosmological observations, particularly the lack of pulsars and radio galaxies, place an upper limit on this mixing parameter. By analyzing how galactic magnetic fields dissipate due to monopole interactions, we suggest that the allowed parameter space can be significantly reduced (to $\epsilon^2 \sim 10^{-6})$, with monolithic monopoles potentially suppressed to fractions of the cosmic dark matter budget.

Transport of materials and signaling within neurons is fundamental to maintaining cell health, preventing apoptosis and pathology, and avoiding dysfunction. Biologically accurate simulation of this process is essential for diagnosing and treating neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's, yet accurate computational results are hindered by uncertainties regarding intra-cellular parameters. To address this limitation, we employ a partial differential equation (PDE) model to simulate neuron traffic and material transport. A rigorous optimization-based inverse methodology is utilized to estimate uncertain parameters by aligning computational simulations with experimental data obtained from electron microscopy of neurons. This capability allows the proposed methodology to faithfully replicate an intracellular transport "traffic jam" characterized by a physical barrier, including the resulting accumulation of protein aggregates.

Hebbian theory explains that the weight of connections between agents increases with the frequency of their simultaneous activity, providing a foundation for learning and adaptability in artificial intelligence to the biological realm of synapses. This research investigates the practical application of such plasticity by extending a previously suggested molecular protocol into a system of interconnected artificial neurons, utilizing a chemical logical AND gate, to emulate the learning process associated with the spiking Heppian neuron. The X-ray free-electron linear oscillator (XFELO) is anticipated to function as a highly coherent, tunable, and reliable x-ray source. In this work, we present analyses of and simulations regarding the sasing and lasing regimes within the XAM, utilizing models grounded in the three-dimensional space charge field and higher-order beam dynamics. Our results reveal that when an XFELO beam undergoes amplification, both transverse and longitudinal coherence can be maintained only if the device operates in the sasing regime, provided the system parameters satisfy strict limitations concerning both geometric configuration and operational conditions. Furthermore, we evaluated these constraints in relation to a state-of-the-art design, performing an order-of-magnitude assessment. Consistent with previous findings, maintaining the XFELO's full coherence demands precise control over a wide range of parameters, necessitating advanced technology in the XAM to achieve stable, high-coherence operation.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) utilizes a hybrid quantum-classical framework for obtaining approximate answers to variational problems, relying on a classical component to optimize quantum circuit parameters. This study introduces a Bayesian optimization procedure to handle this tuning process and evaluates its efficacy against existing global optimizers. The results demonstrate that the proposed method is both quicker and more consistent than competing algorithms, particularly in scenarios dealing with a larger volume of quantum hardware data, often achieving high-fidelity solutions within very few iterations of classical-circuit exchanges. Additionally, by leveraging classical information from prior instances of the same QAOA instance to constrain the prior distribution of future problems, this approach further enhances its convergence speed and solution quality.

Although the mechanism of high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates is not yet fully understood, electron systems on triangular and honeycomb lattices are considered plausible alternative hosts. We investigate the normal state of a two-dimensional triangular-lattice Hubbard model including next-nearest-neighbor hopping, employing full-dynamical mean theory in the local vertex extension alongside exact diagonalization for critical comparisons. By examining the temperature dependence of the magnetic susceptibility, we identify evidence suggesting an antiferromagnetic quantum phase transition occurs at the Hartree-Fock mean field transition line, consistent with cuprate behavior where this line is smoothed out by quantum fluctuations. While exact diagonalization on small clusters supports this convergence, our numerical findings indicate that finite-size effects may misleadingly represent this transition as a Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless type transition on the approach to zero temperature. Conversely, within the normal state, we discover an ordering driven by disorder caused by softening of a commensurate spin density wave mode, which produces a low-energy disordered peak in the spin spectral function. The analysis of the full phase diagram reveals a connection between this physical phenomenon and high-temperature superconductivity in the nearby region.

A key advantage of this approach is that it requires no initially trained parameters, allowing it to generalize across various datasets regardless of differences in vertebrae sizes or positions. A significant portion of the study is dedicated to formulating this alignment as an optimization problem subject to anatomical constraints. A differentiable distance metric is defined to measure alignment based on the spatial distribution of points around the spine, utilizing a derived Gaussian function. This study presents a differentiable kernel that generates a distance field, defined by a Gaussian function, from objects to a linear spine. During optimization, this function evaluates the proximity of scanned points against the model. We introduced a new approach utilizing anatomically specific constraints for localizing and recognizing vertebrae in CT datasets, where a specific differentiable kernel was defined to allow the optimization to use spatial data.

When acoustic waves tunnel through the vacuum separating two nearby piezoelectric materials, they convert into electrical currents that can be measured. This phenomenon, known as mechanical tunneling, is analogous to quantum particle tunneling, where one system's state influences another based on the distance between them, causing wave functions to overlap. Here, we demonstrate that complete tunneling of acoustic energy between two piezo-electric systems occurs at specific systems of tunneling distances, resulting in zero transmission. These zero-dissipation points occur when an integer number of tunnel cycles matches half a wavelength. This effect is governed by wave nature, specifically interference between closely spaced crystal pairs, and is determined by measuring the phase relationship between two nearby crystals as it shifts with frequency. Because this effect is fundamentally wave-based, it offers a robust method to distinguish between wave and particle behavior in tunnel scenarios, with potential future uses in acoustic devices that either block sound entirely or serve as high-precision frequency sensors.

The disintegration of ultra-short-period gas planets situated very close to their stars generates substantial outgassing and debris rings, which can be characterized using mid-infrared excess emission detected by space-based observatories. While current data primarily constrain conditions at altitudes of roughly 0.1 planetary radii above the 1-bar level, upcoming sensitivity enhancements at future facilities aim to probe deeper into outgassing sources. We assessed existing and upcoming instrument capabilities for characterening planetary atmospheres, employing simulations of a disintegrating analog of K2-22 b to determine the detectability of large dust aggregates. Assessments with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWS), a 6.5-meter class telescope, and the Near-Earth Telescope (LBT) are discussed in terms of identifying potential dust aggregates with radii exceeding 0.05 mu.m. We demonstrate that the LBT can combine near-infrared bands through a "complementary strategy" to detect large dust particles within this size regime. Such detection enables reconstruction of the dust-size distribution, yielding insights into atmospheric chemistry and physical conditions. Specifically, our analysis suggests that large silicate particles likely result from the precipitation of condensation processes, indicating high-temperature, high-pressure conditions at depths of approximately 0.02 or 0.03 stellar atmospheric scale heights. Additionally, our model fits suggest a mass loss rate of about $10^{-10}$ mu.m. per year.

I argue that eighteenth-century historians' claims about Galileo are flawed; they overlook the fact that the Italian scientist's true legacy is his demonstration of the limits of mathematical physics. By showing how such an approach cannot address all inquiries, Galileo inadvertently elevated the status of philosophy as an independent discipline, a legacy that persists today.

Recombinations in the early universe influence ionization dynamics and generate secondary electrons and photons, causing deviations in the cosmic ionization fraction and the temperature spectrum of scattering photons from a blackbody shape. Because Gaia and the Kepler mission have recently indicated that the power spectrum of stellar masses is non-Gaussian based on luminosity distributions, examining a potentially non-Gaussian mass distribution generated during recombination becomes significant. We re-examined the power spectrum using the standard Gaussian assumption derived from the Hubble parameter and turned our attention to a Saha model to derive an expected non-Gaussian early-matter mass distribution. Analyzing this scenario in the mass range of $10^{-41}$ to $10^{-40}$ kg, we found that while ionization remains between 20 and 80 percent, the resulting temperature shift is minimal, approximately 0.01%. However, we observed that the power spectrum exhibits a distinct long-end tail featuring an anomalous peak near one solar mass and power augmentation at lower frequencies.

Collisionless magnetic reconnection typically demands kinetic treatments, which are generally applied solely to very small regions yet can complexly model large-scale phenomena such as magnetic island coalescence. In this study, we introduced a hybrid approach combining magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) with adaptively embedded particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations. In this setup, the MHD solution is calculated on a global scale, while the PIC model for magnetic field evolution is applied in select critical cells. The results demonstrate that this technique can efficiently and accurately capture key features of reconnection, including the magnetic field evolution, ion distribution, and the global impact of collisionless effects, all without incurring the high computational costs associated with a fully global PIC simulation.
